About me

Curiosity, quantified

Who I am

Curiosity has always driven my work more than technology itself - AI simply became the best medium to explore difficult questions. I'm an aspiring AI/ML Engineer who enjoys understanding why intelligent systems make the decisions they do, not just how to train them. I'm most excited by problems where research meets real-world impact.

What interests me

I enjoy questions that don't have obvious answers. How do we know a model is fair? When should an AI refuse to answer? Can different models disagree for measurable reasons? These are the kinds of engineering and research problems that keep me curious.

Why AI

I like building things whose behaviour isn't completely obvious from reading the code. You can ask a question in the morning, train a model in the afternoon, and by evening have something that sees, hears, predicts, or reasons in ways that weren't possible before. The most interesting part isn't that they answer questions - it's that they can also be confidently wrong. So they have to be tested, questioned, measured, and continuously improved. That combination of software engineering and scientific experimentation is what makes this field endlessly interesting to me.

What I'm currently learning

Deepening my knowledge of LLMs, exploring Defense Tech applications of AI, and sharpening my prompt engineering - while actively looking for ML Engineer / AI Engineer roles.

LLM Intern

Identifying & quantizing bias in LLMs

The problem: bias-evaluation benchmarks are almost entirely Western-centric, so they miss how bias actually shows up in Indian social, historical, and political context. I helped build a framework to measure it instead of just describing it - across terrorism narratives, territorial issues, and historical events.

Built a batch inference pipeline across 10 open-source LLMs (Mistral-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, OPT-1.3B and others), then layered a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system on top so the team could tell the difference between a model being biased and a model just being wrong. Bias itself was scored across 6 quantitative dimensions - ELO ranking, SAR, semantic similarity, sentiment, response-length bias, and Pairwise Positional Consistency.

Research & Publications

Published work

IDCIoT-2026

Smart AI Multimodal Architecture for Automated Emergency Detection and Alerts

4th International Conference on Intelligent Data Communication Technologies and Internet of Things

The increasing demand for intelligent and proactive emergency response systems exposes the limitations of conventional surveillance setups that rely on manual monitoring and are prone to delayed or missed distress detection. This paper presents a multimodal AI-based emergency alert system integrating audio and video analysis for real-time distress recognition - an audio pipeline built on Librosa preprocessing and YAMNet embeddings feeding a lightweight classifier, and a video pipeline using MediaPipe landmark extraction and LSTM sequence modeling for the "Help Me" hand gesture - fused through a Twilio-based alert layer for rapid, scalable emergency detection in high-risk environments.

AI-Based Emergency
Alerting System

a multimodal AI system that hears screams and sees "help me"

Python TensorFlow Lite YAMNet YOLO-Pose / MediaPipe LSTM · CNN · ANN NTFY
Read the paper (IEEE) →
95%Audio (scream) accuracy
80%Video (gesture) accuracy
3,493Audio embeddings
<1sNTFY alert latency*

*time from confirmed detection to notification push, per the alerting design.

Problem statement

Traditional CCTV infrastructure is passive - it records, but it doesn't understand. It depends entirely on a human operator watching the right feed at the right second, which fails exactly when it matters most. The 2012 Nirbhaya case in Delhi, the 2019 Walmart shooting in the US, the 2018 Surat kidnapping, and a 2022 Mumbai local train harassment case all had cameras rolling - and none of them triggered an alert, because no system was built to interpret distress in real time.

Emergencies don't always look like emergencies to a machine: a scream, a shouted keyword, or - for someone who can't speak out, whether from fear, a speech impairment, or the situation itself - a silent hand gesture. Most prior systems handle only one of these modalities in isolation, and few integrate audio distress detection with visual gesture recognition, especially for something as specific as a universal "Help Me" sign. This project set out to combine both into a single, real-time, automatically-alerting system.

System architecture

Two independent recognition pipelines run in parallel on separate threads and converge into a shared decision layer - either module firing above threshold is enough to trigger an alert.

Audio flow

01

Capture

Microphone input sampled continuously at 16 kHz.

02

Preprocess

Mono conversion, resampling, amplitude normalization to [-1, 1], zero-padding for uniform length.

03

Feature extraction

YAMNet (pretrained on Google AudioSet) generates 1024-D embeddings; temporal mean pooling aggregates them into one fixed-length vector.

04

Classify

Lightweight ANN - Dense(256, ReLU) → Dropout(0.3) → Sigmoid - outputs a distress probability.

Video flow

01

Capture

Webcam frames sampled at a controlled rate (~30 FPS source).

02

Preprocess

Resize, normalize, brightness-correct and denoise each frame to handle lighting/motion-blur variation.

03

Feature extraction

YOLO-Pose / MediaPipe Hands locates 21 hand landmarks per frame; sequences of (x,y) keypoints across 15 frames × 63 features capture motion over time.

04

Classify

LSTM(64) → Dense(32, ReLU) → Sigmoid distinguishes the "Help Me" gesture from normal hand movement.

Dataset

The audio dataset combined scream and non-scream samples, producing 3,493 YAMNet embeddings - 2,631 non-scream and 862 scream - split into train/validation and trained for 30 epochs.

The video dataset was harder: recognizing a specific "Help Me" gesture (not generic hand motion) meant no off-the-shelf dataset fit. It was assembled from RWF-2000 and Real Life Violence datasets (for the "distress" class), UCF50 and HMDB51 (for "normal" movement, to separate activity from violence), and a custom-recorded "Help Me" gesture set augmented with mirror-flipping, rotation, scaling, and brightness adjustment - plus additional gesture clips sourced from YouTube to widen camera-angle and lighting diversity.

Model & accuracy

Audio: scream detection

95% overall classification accuracy on the held-out validation set. Precision, recall, and F1 all stayed above 93% weighted-average, with the non-scream class scoring slightly higher due to class imbalance (152/172 screams and 511/527 non-screams correctly classified).

Video: "Help Me" gesture

80% overall classification accuracy. Precision/recall/F1 were lower for the distress class (0.70 / 0.75 / 0.724) than non-distress (0.86 / 0.826 / 0.843) - largely a reflection of how much harder gesture recognition is under real-world viewpoint, occlusion, and motion-blur variation.

Alert system

Detection alone doesn't help anyone - so the moment either module crosses its 0.50 probability threshold (and holds for a short minimum duration, to suppress single-frame noise), the system publishes an alert to an NTFY topic over HTTP. Any device subscribed to that topic - phone, desktop, monitoring dashboard - gets the notification instantly, with a timestamp and event type attached, no manual monitoring required.

Challenges

No existing dataset for the exact gesture. Generic hand-gesture datasets exist; a dataset for the specific universal "Help Me" sign, across enough camera angles and lighting conditions to generalize, did not. That meant building it from scratch through custom recording and augmentation.
Fusing two modalities without losing accuracy. Running audio and video inference concurrently, then merging their outputs into one reliable decision, required careful threading and threshold tuning to avoid one module's noise dragging down the other's precision.

The problem

Most carbon footprint calculators rely on static, average-based coefficients - they don't adapt to an individual's actual behaviour, and they give little in the way of personalized, actionable feedback. This project set out to replace static estimation with a machine-learning approach that learns from real lifestyle and behavioural data, so a user's number actually reflects their transport habits, energy use, and lifestyle choices - and tells them where their footprint is really coming from.

ML models used

Two complementary models feed an ensemble: Linear Regression, chosen for its interpretability - its coefficients show directly how much a feature like kilometers driven per week or diet type affects the total footprint - and Random Forest Regression, which captures non-linear feature interactions without needing standardized input, and is more robust to outliers. The ensemble averages both, balancing Linear Regression's low variance/high bias against Random Forest's low bias/higher variance for more stable overall predictions.

Beyond the total-footprint model, three category-specific Random Forest regressors were trained separately for Transportation CO₂, Home Energy CO₂, and Lifestyle CO₂ - giving the app an interpretable breakdown, not just a single number.

Results

The dataset - 673 samples across 10 features (transportation habits, energy usage, lifestyle factors) - was cleaned with median imputation, categorical encoding, and StandardScaler normalization, then split 70:30 for train/test. Performance was measured with RMSE and R²:

Interestingly, Linear Regression edged out both Random Forest and the ensemble on raw R² here - but the ensemble still delivered the most stable predictions across the full sample range, which matters more for a tool people will use repeatedly with different inputs.

Features

Category breakdown, not just a total. Transportation, home energy, and lifestyle emissions are shown separately, so a user can see exactly where their footprint is concentrated.
Gauge and pie chart visualizations. Built for non-technical users - the app translates raw kg-CO₂ numbers into visuals that are easy to read at a glance.
Personalized reduction recommendations. Category-level predictions drive suggestions targeted at whatever is actually driving a given user's footprint, rather than generic advice.
